While I don't think it'll ever disappear completely (console makers can always produce their own games), it no longer justifies purchasing an entire console. That since time is finite, and that the ultimate goal is to play the games you enjoy most AND that you have time for, a PC absolutely guarantees an endless library to choose from, whereas a console's library will always be finite. Of course I want to play the game, but I won't buy an entire console for it, whether I can afford it or not. What happens afterwards? I just end up with a big brick in my media console. I do still have an older console connected, but that's because it is technically one of the better blu-Ray players sub $1,000, and as such I still get constant use out of it. Please understand, that me saying all of this is bittersweet. Everything I wrote before, I did so begrudgingly. I grew with video games. Owned most every system from early home consoles to handhelds. Hell, just the other weekend, and with minimal effort, I turned a handheld into an emulator for multiple classic systems, complete with hundreds of roms (my entire game library growing up). Just so everyone understands what's going on: On a recent date, a major lottery added numbers to the white balls and removed power balls. So, what used to have specific chances of winning, now has different chances of winning. **This** **means** **everyone**'**s** **chances** **of** **winning** **have** **decreased** **by** **a significant percentage**. This is only the first of many more billion dollar jackpots. If you're interested in how to calculate the odds yourself, here it is (in short): First, if you want to know the odds of something, you multiply them. 1 coin landing heads versus two coins landing heads is the chance of (1/2) versus (1/2)x(1/2)=(1x1)/(2x2)=(1/4), 1 in four chance both coins land heads. Now we apply to this the lottery, but on a much bigger scale. Your first number has five chances to be picked, because we are going to draw five times from a larger pool of numbers. It can be drawn first, second, third, fourth, or fifth. Five chances. So, it has a chance of 5/69. Your second number only has four chances to be picked, as one chance was used to. Likewise, one ball not matching your second number was already removed on the first drawing, so instead of 69 balls to choose from, there are 68. So, your second number has a 4/68 chance of being picked. Your third number has 3 chances out of 67. Your fourth has a 2 in 66. And fifth a 1 in 65. The powerball is drawn from a separate pool. No matter the outcome of the first five drawings, your powerball always has 1/26 chance of being drawn. Putting it all together, using the coin flip principle from earlier, (5/69)x(4/68)x(3/67)x(2/66)x(1/65)x(1/26)= (5x4x3x2x1x1) / (69x68x67x66x65x64) = which equals some tiny ugly number (let's call this a t.u.n.). To make this number easier to talk about we divide 1 by tiny ugly number. 1/t.u.n.=292,201,338. That's 292,201,338 different combinations of numbers, or for you, 1 in 292,201,338 chances of winning for every ticket you buy. As for the percent decrease, there are a few approaches you can take to figure this out. Either 1 - (292M-175M)/175M. Or 1 - (new t.u.n.)/(old t.u.n.). In our case, we got a ~40% drop.
